title: Staying between
hook: walking between traditions asks for extra respect: tag the source, don't borrow the sacred carelessly; Tertullian and Augustine argue it out
tomorrow: Abraham threw a guest out of his tent. what happened next?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: ask them. Every tradition keeps its own door, and its own people know it. Today, for those who stay outside every door, walking between.

A playlist called calm: a chant from a monastery, a Sufi song, a singing bowl, none of them labeled. Borrowing is easy now. Early Christian writers argued over it. Tertullian, a sharp-tongued writer from Carthage, put the question in a line, here in an old public-domain English translation: "What indeed has Athens to do with Jerusalem?" Athens meant the philosophers. Jerusalem meant the faith. His answer: nothing at all.
screen: `A PLAYLIST WITH NO LABELS.` → `WHAT HAS ATHENS TO DO WITH JERUSALEM?` → `TERTULLIAN: NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Tertullian's case at its strongest: mixing sources blurs them. He saw the heresies of his day growing out of philosophy, and wanted the faith kept plain. Pour the philosophers into the faith and you get something that is neither. Keep them apart, so each stays itself. Augustine saw it another way, and he used a story to say it. When Israel left Egypt, Exodus says, "they borrowed of the Egyptians jewels of silver, and jewels of gold," and carried them out. Augustine read that as permission: whatever is true and good in the philosophers belongs to God, so take it and put it to good use. But notice how he takes it. He doesn't hide where it came from: he names the philosophers, the Platonists above all, and says their gold was God's all along, scattered everywhere. Both views sit in the Christian library, and each has its heirs. For someone walking between traditions, they make a fair pair of rules. From Augustine: you may carry what's true from one house to another, and say where you found it. From Tertullian: don't blend it into mush, and don't use the sacred as decoration. Put together, that's today's practice: tag the source. A mantra, a candle, a mala: each has a home. Say where it comes from, what it means there, and who keeps it.
screen: `TERTULLIAN: KEEP THEM APART.` · `EGYPT'S JEWELS OF GOLD.` · `AUGUSTINE: TAKE IT, STILL NAMED.` · `CARRY, DON'T BLEND.` · then, large: `EVERY BORROWING HAS A HOME.`

segments.voice: Look at one thing near you that came from a tradition not your own: a candle, a bead, a word you use, a song. Ask it three questions in silence: where are you from, what do you mean there, and who keeps you? If you can't answer, that's the borrowing to check.
Staying between: walking among traditions without joining one, and with extra respect. Tag the source; don't borrow the sacred carelessly.
For the road: tag the source, and say where you found it. That's day 1704.

howItsDone: Christian thinkers debated how to use learning from outside the faith, from Tertullian's 'Athens and Jerusalem' to Augustine's 'gold of Egypt'. On a personal path drawn from many sources, each borrowed practice is named with its source, its meaning there and the people who keep it.
